title: Authentication & Security
summary: Learn how logins really work and how to protect them: password hashing, sessions, JWT, OAuth and OpenID Connect, MFA, passkeys, permissions and defenses against common attacks.

lessons.title: Authentication vs authorization
lessons.summary: Separate the two big questions: who are you, and what are you allowed to do?

slides.title: Two different questions
slides.text:
- **Authentication** (AuthN): *Who are you?*
- **Authorization** (AuthZ): *What may you do?*

First we identify, then we decide.
slides.narration: Security on the web starts with two questions that sound alike but are very different. Authentication asks who you are. Authorization asks what you are allowed to do. A system always answers the first one before the second.

slides.title: An airport analogy
slides.text:
- Showing your **passport** = authentication
- Your **boarding pass** for seat 12A on one flight = authorization

A valid passport does not let you board every plane.
slides.narration: Think of an airport. Showing your passport proves who you are, that is authentication. Your boarding pass says which flight and seat you may use, that is authorization. Having a valid passport does not let you board any plane you like.

slides.title: Factors of authentication
slides.text:
Proof can be something you:
- **know**: password, PIN
- **have**: phone, security key
- **are**: fingerprint, face

Using two or more = **MFA**.
slides.narration: There are three kinds of proof, called factors. Something you know, like a password. Something you have, like a phone or a security key. And something you are, like a fingerprint. Combining factors from different groups is called multi factor authentication.

slides.title: In HTTP terms
slides.text:
- not authenticated → **401 Unauthorized**
- authenticated but not allowed → **403 Forbidden**

(Yes, the name "401 Unauthorized" really means *unauthenticated*.)
slides.narration: On the web, the two failures have their own status codes. Four oh one means we do not know who you are, so please log in. Four oh three means we know exactly who you are, and the answer is still no. The name of four oh one is a historical mix up, which is why it confuses everyone.

slides.title: The road ahead
slides.text:
1. Passwords and hashing
2. Sessions, cookies, tokens
3. OAuth and OpenID Connect
4. MFA and passkeys
5. Roles and permissions
6. Attacks, defenses and secrets
slides.narration: In this course we will walk the whole path. We start with passwords and how to store them, then how users stay logged in, then signing in with other providers, stronger login with MFA and passkeys, permissions, and finally the attacks you must defend against.

lessons.notes:
## Two questions

| | Authentication (AuthN) | Authorization (AuthZ) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Who are you? | What are you allowed to do? |
| Example | Log in with password + code | Only admins may delete users |
| Failure code | **401** Unauthorized | **403** Forbidden |
| When | First | After authentication, on every action |

## Factors

- **Knowledge**: password, PIN, security question (weak).
- **Possession**: phone app, hardware security key, smart card.
- **Inherence**: fingerprint, face, voice.

**Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** combines factors from *different* groups. Two passwords is still one factor.

## Identity, credentials, sessions

- An **identity** is an account (e.g. user 42, `ana@example.com`).
- A **credential** proves you own it (password, passkey, code).
- After a successful login, the server gives you a **session** or **token**, so you do not need to log in on every request.

## Why it matters

Most serious breaches involve stolen credentials or broken authorization checks. Getting these basics right protects your users more than any fancy feature.

## Golden rules

1. Authenticate with strong, phishing-resistant methods when possible.
2. Authorize **on the server**, for **every** request and every record.
3. Deny by default: if no rule allows it, refuse.
4. Use well-tested libraries and providers; do not invent your own crypto.

quiz.q: Checking whether a logged-in user may edit a document is...
quiz.explain: Deciding what an identified user may do is authorization.

quiz.q: Password + SMS code is an example of...
quiz.explain: It combines something you know with something you have.

quiz.q: Which status code means "we know who you are, but no"?
quiz.explain: 403 Forbidden is an authorization failure.

lessons.task: Pick an app you use (a school portal, a bank, a game). List how it authenticates you (which factors) and three things it authorizes differently for different users (for example, teachers vs students).

lessons.title: Passwords done right
lessons.summary: Learn modern password rules: long, not common, no forced complexity tricks.

slides.title: Passwords are still everywhere
slides.text:
Passwords are easy to build but easy to steal:
- phishing
- reuse across sites
- leaked databases
- guessing

Good rules reduce the damage.
slides.narration: Passwords are still the most common way to log in, even though they have many problems. People reuse them, attackers phish them, and leaked databases expose them. Good password rules will not fix everything, but they cut down the damage a lot.

slides.title: What modern guidance says
slides.text:
NIST SP 800-63B (2025):
- **length** matters most: at least **15** characters if it is the only factor (8 with MFA)
- allow at least **64** characters, spaces and emoji
- **no** forced symbol/number rules
- **no** forced regular changes
slides.narration: Modern guidance from NIST, the US standards body, turned old advice upside down. Length matters most. Passwords used alone should be at least fifteen characters, and you should allow long passphrases with spaces. Forcing symbols and changing passwords every ninety days just makes people choose predictable patterns.

slides.title: Block bad passwords
slides.text:
Check every new password against:
- lists of **common** passwords
- **breached** passwords (e.g. Have I Been Pwned, k-anonymity API)
- the **username** or site name
slides.narration: Instead of composition rules, block known bad passwords. Reject the most common ones, passwords that appeared in breaches, and anything containing the username. The Have I Been Pwned service lets you check breaches without ever sending the full password.

slides.title: Help users
slides.text:
- show a **strength meter** (e.g. zxcvbn)
- allow **paste** so password managers work
- offer a "show password" toggle
- give one clear error at a time
slides.narration: Make good passwords easy. Allow pasting so password managers work, show a strength meter, and let users reveal what they typed. Clear, friendly messages beat a wall of red rules.

slides.title: Checker in Python
slides.text: A tiny rule checker:
slides.narration: Here is the core of a checker in Python. It collects problems in a list, so the user sees all of them at once.

lessons.notes:
## Modern password policy

Based on NIST SP 800-63B (revision 4, 2025) and OWASP guidance:

- **Minimum length**: 15 characters when the password is the only factor; 8 when it is combined with MFA.
- **Maximum length**: allow at least 64 characters.
- **Any characters**: spaces, Unicode and emoji are fine.
- **No composition rules** like "must contain a symbol". They lead to `Password1!`.
- **No forced periodic changes**. Force a change only when there is evidence of compromise.
- **Block lists**: reject common, expected or breached passwords and ones containing the username.
- **No password hints** and no "security questions".
- **Rate-limit** login attempts (covered later).

## Checking breached passwords safely

Have I Been Pwned's *Pwned Passwords* API uses **k-anonymity**: you hash the password with SHA-1, send only the first 5 hex characters, and compare the returned suffixes locally. The full password never leaves your server.

## Example

```python
COMMON = {'passwordpassword', '123456789012345', 'iloveyouiloveyou'}

def problems(pw, user):
    p = []
    if len(pw) < 15: p.append('too short (minimum 15 characters)')
    if len(pw) > 64: p.append('too long (maximum 64 characters)')
    if pw.lower() in COMMON: p.append('too common')
    if user and user.lower() in pw.lower(): p.append('contains the username')
    return p
```

## Better than passwords

Password managers, MFA and **passkeys** (later in this course) are the real long-term fix. A good password policy is your baseline, not your finish line.

quiz.q: Which rule follows modern NIST guidance?
options: Force a password change every 90 days
Check new passwords against breached lists
quiz.explain: NIST recommends block lists of compromised passwords instead of complexity and rotation rules.

quiz.q: Why allow pasting into password fields?
options: So password managers can fill long random passwords
quiz.explain: Blocking paste discourages password managers and leads to weaker passwords.

quiz.q: What is most important for password strength?
quiz.explain: Length adds the most guessing difficulty; long passphrases are strong and memorable.

exercise.title: Password rules checker
exercise.prompt:
Line 1 of standard input is the **password**, line 2 is the **username** (may be empty). Do not strip spaces inside the password; only remove the newline.

Check these rules **in this order** and print one line for every rule that fails:

1. fewer than 15 characters: `too short (minimum 15 characters)`
2. more than 64 characters: `too long (maximum 64 characters)`
3. lowercase password is in `{"passwordpassword", "123456789012345", "qwertyuiopasdfgh", "iloveyouiloveyou", "correcthorsebatterystaple"}`: `too common`
4. username is not empty and appears in the password (ignore case): `contains the username`
5. password is not empty and every character is the same: `one repeated character`

If nothing fails, print `OK`.
exercise.starter:
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
password = lines[0]
username = lines[1].strip() if len(lines) > 1 else ''

# check the rules and print the problems

tests.input:
my name is Ana and I like tea
ana

tests.output:
too long (maximum 64 characters)
contains the username
one repeated character

too short (minimum 15 characters)
contains the username

lessons.title: Hashing and salting passwords
lessons.summary: Store passwords so that even a stolen database does not reveal them.

slides.title: Never store plain passwords
slides.text:
If your database leaks, plain passwords are instantly usable, **on other sites too**.

Store a **hash** instead: a one-way fingerprint.
slides.narration: The first rule of password storage: never store the password itself. Databases leak, and because people reuse passwords, one leak can unlock accounts on many other sites. Instead we store a hash, a one way fingerprint of the password.

slides.title: What a hash is
slides.text:
- same input → same output
- tiny change → totally different output
- **cannot** be reversed

At login: hash the attempt and **compare**.
slides.narration: A hash function turns any input into a fixed size fingerprint. The same input always gives the same output, a tiny change gives a completely different one, and you cannot run it backwards. At login, you hash what the user typed and compare it with the stored hash.

slides.title: Why add salt
slides.text:
Same password → same hash → attackers use **precomputed tables** and spot users with equal passwords.

A **salt** is a random value, unique per user, mixed in before hashing and stored next to the hash.
slides.narration: Without salt, everyone with the password sunshine has the same hash, and attackers can use giant precomputed tables. A salt is a random value created for each user and mixed in before hashing. It is not secret; it is stored right next to the hash, but it makes every hash unique.

slides.title: Fast hashes are wrong here
slides.text:
SHA-256 is **too fast**: GPUs try billions per second.

Use a **slow, memory-hard** password hash:
- **Argon2id** (first choice)
- **scrypt**
- **bcrypt** (fine, 72-byte limit)
- PBKDF2 (when FIPS is required)
slides.narration: Plain SHA two fifty six is great for files, but far too fast for passwords: a graphics card can try billions of guesses per second. Password hashing functions are deliberately slow and use lots of memory. Argon2id is the first choice today, with scrypt and bcrypt as solid alternatives, and PBKDF2 where government standards require it.

slides.title: In practice
slides.text: Libraries add the salt and settings for you:
slides.code:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()                # Argon2id, safe defaults
stored = ph.hash('purple monkey dishwasher')
print(stored[:30])                   # $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$...

ph.verify(stored, 'purple monkey dishwasher')  # True or raises
slides.narration: In real code you use a library that handles salt and settings and stores them all in one string. Here is argon2 in Python. Notice that verify does the comparison for you.

slides.title: Compare in constant time
slides.text:
Use `hmac.compare_digest(a, b)`, not `a == b`.

`==` can stop at the first different byte, leaking timing information.
slides.narration: One last detail. When you compare hashes yourself, use a constant time comparison such as h m a c dot compare digest. A normal equals check may stop early at the first difference, and careful attackers can measure that tiny delay.

lessons.notes:
## Store hashes, not passwords

**Hash**: a one-way function. Given the hash you cannot get the password back; you can only guess passwords and hash each guess.

At **sign-up**: create a random salt, compute `hash = H(salt, password)`, store `salt` and `hash`.
At **login**: load the salt, compute `H(salt, attempt)`, compare with the stored hash in constant time.

## Salt

- Random, at least 16 bytes, unique per password (`secrets.token_bytes(16)`).
- Stored next to the hash; it is not a secret.
- Defeats precomputed **rainbow tables** and hides users with equal passwords.

A **pepper** is an extra secret key kept outside the database (e.g. in a secret manager). It is optional extra protection.

## Choose a password hashing function

| Algorithm | Notes (OWASP 2025 guidance) |
|---|---|
| **Argon2id** | First choice. Minimum e.g. 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 lane. |
| **scrypt** | Good alternative, memory-hard. |
| **bcrypt** | Widely supported; cost 10 or more; inputs over 72 bytes are truncated. |
| **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256** | Use when FIPS compliance is required; about 600,000 iterations. |

**Never** use plain MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256 for passwords.

## Python with the standard library

```python
import hashlib, hmac, secrets
salt = secrets.token_bytes(16)
h = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', b'my long passphrase', salt, 600_000)
ok = hmac.compare_digest(h, hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', b'attempt', salt, 600_000))
```

For new projects prefer the `argon2-cffi` package (`PasswordHasher`) or `bcrypt`. Its output string stores the algorithm, settings and salt together, so you can raise the cost later and **rehash** on the next successful login.
lessons.example:
import hashlib, secrets

for pw in ['sunshine', 'sunshine']:
    salt = secrets.token_hex(8)
    h = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', pw.encode(), bytes.fromhex(salt), 100_000).hex()
    print(salt, h[:24])
# Same password, different salts -> different hashes.

quiz.q: What is a salt?
options: A secret key stored in the code
A random value unique per user, stored with the hash
quiz.explain: A salt is random per password and stored alongside the hash; it need not be secret.

quiz.q: Why is plain SHA-256 a poor choice for passwords?
options: It is too fast, so guessing is cheap
quiz.explain: Fast hashes let attackers try billions of guesses per second.

quiz.q: Which is the recommended first choice for new systems?
quiz.explain: Argon2id is memory-hard and recommended by OWASP.

exercise.title: Verify a login
exercise.prompt:
Your database stores a **salt** and a **hash** for a user. Standard input has three lines:

1. the salt as hex
2. the stored hash as hex
3. the password the user just typed

Compute `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', password_bytes, salt_bytes, 1000)` (UTF-8 password, salt from `bytes.fromhex`) and compare it with the stored hash using `hmac.compare_digest`. Print `Access granted` or `Access denied`.

(1000 iterations keeps this exercise fast; real systems use about 600,000 for PBKDF2, or Argon2id.)
exercise.starter:
import sys, hashlib, hmac

salt_hex, stored_hex, attempt = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')[:3]

# hash the attempt and compare
exercise.solution:
import sys, hashlib, hmac

salt_hex, stored_hex, attempt = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')[:3]
salt = bytes.fromhex(salt_hex.strip())
stored = bytes.fromhex(stored_hex.strip())
h = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', attempt.rstrip('\r').encode('utf-8'), salt, 1000)
print('Access granted' if hmac.compare_digest(h, stored) else 'Access denied')

modules.title: Staying logged in: sessions, tokens, OAuth

lessons.title: Sessions and cookies
lessons.summary: Keep users logged in with server-side sessions and secure cookie settings.

slides.title: HTTP forgets everything
slides.text:
HTTP is **stateless**: each request stands alone.

After login, how does the server know the next request is still you?
slides.narration: HTTP has no memory. Each request arrives on its own, so after you log in, the server needs a way to recognize your next requests. The classic answer is a session stored on the server and a cookie stored in the browser.

slides.title: Session flow
slides.text:
1. Login succeeds
2. Server creates a random **session ID** and stores `{id → user 42}`
3. Response: `Set-Cookie: sid=...`
4. Browser sends `Cookie: sid=...` on every request
5. Server looks up the user
slides.narration: Here is the flow. After a correct password, the server creates a long random session id and remembers which user it belongs to, in memory, a database or Redis. It sends the id in a Set Cookie header. The browser then automatically includes it with each request, and the server looks it up.

slides.title: Cookie attributes
slides.text:
`Set-Cookie: sid=Xk9..; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600`

- **HttpOnly**: JavaScript cannot read it
- **Secure**: HTTPS only
- **SameSite**: limits cross-site sending
slides.narration: The cookie attributes do the heavy lifting. Http only hides the cookie from JavaScript, which protects it from cross site scripting. Secure sends it only over HTTPS. Same site controls whether it is sent with requests coming from other websites, an important defense against cross site request forgery.

slides.title: SameSite values
slides.text:
- **Strict**: never sent from other sites
- **Lax**: sent on top-level links (GET), not on cross-site POSTs; browser default
- **None**: always sent; **requires Secure**
slides.narration: Same site has three values. Strict never sends the cookie on requests that start on another site. Lax, the default in modern browsers, allows normal links but blocks cross site form posts. None sends it everywhere and must be combined with Secure.

slides.title: Session hygiene
slides.text:
- IDs from a **secure random** generator (128+ bits)
- **new ID after login** (stops session fixation)
- idle and absolute **timeouts**
- logout **deletes** the server session
slides.narration: A few habits keep sessions safe. Generate ids with a secure random generator. Issue a fresh id right after login, so an attacker cannot plant one beforehand. Expire sessions after inactivity and after a maximum lifetime, and destroy the session on the server when the user logs out.

lessons.notes:
## Why sessions

HTTP is stateless. A **session** links many requests to one logged-in user.

```
POST /login  (email + password)
← 200 OK
  Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=f3K9...; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

GET /account
  Cookie: __Host-sid=f3K9...
← 200 OK (server looked up sid → user 42)
```

## Server-side session store

| Store | Good for |
|---|---|
| Memory | one dev server only |
| Redis / Valkey | fast, shared between many servers |
| Database table | simple, durable |

## Cookie attributes

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `HttpOnly` | not readable by `document.cookie` (limits XSS damage) |
| `Secure` | only sent over HTTPS |
| `SameSite=Lax/Strict/None` | controls cross-site sending (CSRF defense); `None` requires `Secure` |
| `Max-Age` / `Expires` | lifetime; without them it is a session cookie |
| `Path`, `Domain` | where the cookie is sent |
| `__Host-` prefix | forces `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain` |

## Creating IDs in Python

```python
import secrets
session_id = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)   # 256 random bits
```

Never use `random` for security; it is predictable.

## Lifecycle

- **Rotate** the ID on login and on privilege change.
- **Idle timeout** (e.g. 30 minutes) and **absolute timeout** (e.g. 12 hours, or longer with "remember me").
- **Logout**: delete the server-side record and clear the cookie.
- Offer "log out of all devices" by deleting all of the user's sessions.

Sessions are simple and easy to revoke, which makes them a great default for websites.

quiz.q: What does the HttpOnly flag do?
options: Sends the cookie only over HTTP
Stops JavaScript from reading the cookie
quiz.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, limiting damage from XSS.

quiz.q: Why issue a new session ID after login?
quiz.explain: An attacker might have planted a known ID before login; rotating it defeats that.

quiz.q: SameSite=None requires which other attribute?
quiz.explain: Browsers reject SameSite=None cookies that are not also Secure.

exercise.title: Audit a Set-Cookie header
exercise.prompt:
Standard input is one `Set-Cookie` header value, for example
`sid=abc123; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`.

Parts are separated by `;`. The first part is `name=value`. Attribute names are **case-insensitive**.

Print:

```
name: <cookie name>
HttpOnly: yes|no
Secure: yes|no
SameSite: Strict|Lax|None|missing
verdict: OK|WEAK
```

Print the SameSite value with only its first letter uppercase (`lax` → `Lax`). The verdict is `OK` only if HttpOnly and Secure are present **and** SameSite is `Strict` or `Lax`; otherwise `WEAK`.
exercise.starter:
import sys

header = sys.stdin.read().strip()
parts = [p.strip() for p in header.split(';')]
name = parts[0].split('=')[0]

# look at parts[1:]
exercise.solution:
import sys

header = sys.stdin.read().strip()
parts = [p.strip() for p in header.split(';') if p.strip()]
name = parts[0].split('=', 1)[0]
http_only = secure = False
same_site = 'missing'
for attr in parts[1:]:
    key, _, value = attr.partition('=')
    key = key.strip().lower()
    if key == 'httponly':
        http_only = True
    elif key == 'secure':
        secure = True
    elif key == 'samesite':
        same_site = value.strip().capitalize()

ok = http_only and secure and same_site in ('Strict', 'Lax')
print('name: ' + name)
print('HttpOnly: ' + ('yes' if http_only else 'no'))
print('Secure: ' + ('yes' if secure else 'no'))
print('SameSite: ' + same_site)
print('verdict: ' + ('OK' if ok else 'WEAK'))

tests.output:
name: sid
HttpOnly: yes
Secure: yes
SameSite: Lax
verdict: OK

name: theme
HttpOnly: no
Secure: no
SameSite: missing
verdict: WEAK

name: __Host-sid
HttpOnly: yes
Secure: yes
SameSite: Strict
verdict: OK

name: track
HttpOnly: yes
Secure: yes
SameSite: None
verdict: WEAK

name: token
HttpOnly: yes
Secure: no
SameSite: Lax
verdict: WEAK

lessons.title: Tokens and JWT
lessons.summary: Understand bearer tokens, read a JSON Web Token, and learn when to use one.

slides.title: Tokens instead of cookies
slides.text:
A **bearer token** is a string the client sends:

`Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...`

Whoever **bears** it is let in, so protect it like a password.
slides.narration: Instead of a cookie, some clients send a token in the Authorization header. It is called a bearer token because whoever holds it gets access, just like a concert ticket. That makes tokens convenient for mobile apps and APIs, and dangerous if stolen.

slides.title: What a JWT looks like
slides.text:
A **JSON Web Token** has 3 parts joined by dots:

`header.payload.signature`

Each part is **base64url** encoded.
slides.narration: A JSON Web Token, or JWT, is a popular token format. It has three parts separated by dots: a header, a payload and a signature. The first two are just JSON encoded with base64url, a URL safe variant of base64.

slides.title: Encoded is not encrypted
slides.text:
Anyone can **decode** the payload. Never put secrets in it.

The **signature** proves it was not changed. **Always verify** it before trusting any claim.
slides.narration: Here is the most important point: base64url is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can read a JWT payload, so never put secrets inside. What protects the token is the signature. The server must verify the signature, the algorithm and the expiry before trusting a single claim.

slides.title: Standard claims
slides.text:
- `sub`: subject (user ID)
- `exp`: expires at (Unix seconds)
- `iat`: issued at
- `iss`: issuer, `aud`: audience

Algorithms: **HS256** (shared secret), **RS256 / ES256** (public/private key)
slides.narration: JWTs use short standard claim names. Sub is the user, exp is when it expires, iat is when it was issued, iss is who issued it and aud is who it is meant for. HS256 signs with a shared secret, while RS256 and ES256 use a private key to sign and a public key to verify, which is ideal when many services must check tokens.

slides.title: Decode in Python
slides.text: Add back the `=` padding, then decode:
slides.narration: Decoding the payload in Python takes three steps: split on the dots, add back the padding that base64url drops, and parse the JSON. Remember, this only reads the token, it does not verify it.

slides.title: Use JWTs wisely
slides.text:
- short-lived **access tokens** (5-15 min) + **refresh tokens** (rotated)
- hard to **revoke** before expiry
- reject `alg: none`, pin the expected algorithm
- use a library: **PyJWT**, jose
slides.narration: JWTs are hard to cancel once issued, so keep access tokens short lived and pair them with refresh tokens that rotate on each use. Always pin the expected algorithm and reject tokens that say alg none. And use a trusted library like PyJWT rather than writing verification by hand in production.

lessons.notes:
## Bearer tokens

```
GET /api/me
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiJ9.k3J...
```

## JWT structure

`base64url(header) . base64url(payload) . base64url(signature)`

- **Header**: algorithm and type, e.g. `{"alg":"ES256","typ":"JWT"}`.
- **Payload**: claims such as `sub`, `exp`, `iat`, `iss`, `aud`, plus your own (`role`).
- **Signature**: `HMAC-SHA256(secret, header.payload)` for HS256, or an RSA/ECDSA signature for RS256/ES256.

base64url uses `-` and `_` instead of `+` and `/` and drops `=` padding. Decoding it is trivial: **a JWT is signed, not encrypted** (encrypted tokens, JWE, exist but are less common).

## Verifying correctly (PyJWT)

```python
import jwt
claims = jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=['ES256'], audience='api.example.com')
```

The library checks the signature, `exp`, `nbf` and `aud`. Always pass an explicit `algorithms` list.

## Common mistakes

- Accepting `alg: none` or letting the token choose the algorithm.
- Storing secrets or personal data in the payload.
- Long-lived tokens that cannot be revoked.
- Weak HS256 secrets (use 32+ random bytes).
- Storing tokens in `localStorage`, where XSS can read them. For browser apps, an HttpOnly cookie is usually safer.

## Sessions or JWT?

| | Server session | JWT |
|---|---|---|
| Revoke instantly | easy | hard (wait for expiry or keep a deny list) |
| Server lookup per request | yes | no |
| Best for | classic websites | APIs, mobile, service-to-service, OAuth/OIDC |

quiz.q: Can anyone read the payload of a signed JWT?
options: Yes, it is only base64url encoded
quiz.explain: The payload is encoded, not encrypted; the signature only prevents changes.

quiz.q: What does the `exp` claim hold?
options: The expiry time in Unix seconds
quiz.explain: exp is a NumericDate: seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC.

quiz.q: Why keep access tokens short-lived?
options: They are hard to revoke before they expire
Long tokens do not fit in headers
quiz.explain: A stolen JWT stays valid until exp, so short lifetimes limit the damage.

exercise.title: Inspect and verify a JWT
exercise.prompt:

4. Then one line per payload claim, sorted by key: `key = value`, where strings are printed as-is and other values with `json.dumps`.

Remember to add `=` padding before decoding base64url.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
lessons.summary: See how "Sign in with Google" works and why OAuth is about access, not identity.

slides.title: The problem OAuth solves
slides.text:
A printing app wants your Google Photos.

**Bad**: give it your Google password.
**Good**: Google gives it a limited **access token** you approved.
slides.narration: Imagine a photo printing app that needs your pictures from a cloud service. In the bad old days you would give it your password. OAuth fixes this. You approve limited access, and the app receives a token that can only do what you allowed, which you can revoke at any time.

slides.title: The four roles
slides.text:
- **Resource owner**: you
- **Client**: the app asking for access
- **Authorization server**: issues tokens (e.g. Google, Microsoft Entra ID)
- **Resource server**: the API holding the data
slides.narration: OAuth names four roles. You are the resource owner. The app is the client. The authorization server checks who you are and issues tokens, and the resource server is the API that holds your data and accepts those tokens.

slides.title: Authorization code flow + PKCE
slides.text:
1. App sends you to the auth server with `scope` and a **code challenge**
2. You log in and **consent**
3. Redirect back with a short-lived **code**
4. App swaps code + **code verifier** for tokens
5. App calls the API with the access token
slides.narration: The recommended flow is the authorization code flow with PKCE. The app redirects you to the authorization server, you log in and approve. You are sent back with a one time code, and the app exchanges that code, plus a secret verifier only it knows, for tokens. PKCE stops attackers who intercept the code from using it.

slides.title: OAuth is not login
slides.text:
OAuth answers: *may this app access X?*

**OpenID Connect (OIDC)** adds identity on top:
- scope `openid`
- an **ID token** (a JWT) saying who logged in
- a `/userinfo` endpoint
slides.narration: Here is a common confusion. OAuth by itself is about authorization, granting access. It does not define how to tell the app who you are. OpenID Connect is a thin layer on top that adds identity: ask for the openid scope and you get an ID token, a signed JWT describing the user.

slides.title: Rules for 2026
slides.text:
- use **authorization code + PKCE** for every client type
- **implicit** and **password** grants are deprecated
- validate **state**, **nonce**, issuer, audience
- exact-match **redirect URIs**
- prefer a certified library or identity provider
slides.narration: Modern best practice, captured in OAuth two point one and the OAuth security best current practice, is simple. Use the code flow with PKCE everywhere, and never the old implicit or password grants. Validate state and nonce values, register exact redirect addresses, and lean on certified libraries or identity providers.

lessons.notes:
## OAuth 2.0 in one sentence

OAuth lets a user give an app **limited, revocable access** to their data on another service **without sharing their password**.

## Roles

| Role | Example |
|---|---|
| Resource owner | You |
| Client | A photo-printing app |
| Authorization server | accounts.google.com, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak |
| Resource server | Google Photos API |

## Authorization code flow with PKCE

1. The client makes a random **code_verifier** and sends its SHA-256 hash (**code_challenge**) with the redirect:
   `GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&scope=openid%20photos.read&state=xyz&code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256`
2. The user logs in at the authorization server and approves the **scopes**.
3. The server redirects back: `https://app.example.com/callback?code=abc&state=xyz`.
4. The client checks `state`, then POSTs `code` + `code_verifier` to the **token endpoint**.
5. It receives an **access token** (and maybe a **refresh token** and an **ID token**).
6. It calls the API with `Authorization: Bearer <access token>`.

## Scopes

Scopes limit what a token can do: `photos.read`, `calendar.write`. Ask for the fewest possible.

## OpenID Connect

OIDC is an identity layer on OAuth 2.0:

- Request scope **`openid`** (plus `profile`, `email`).
- Receive an **ID token**: a JWT with `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `nonce`, and maybe `email`.
- Validate its signature (keys from the provider's JWKS URL), issuer, audience, expiry and nonce.

Use `sub` + `iss` as the stable user identifier, not the email.

## Other flows

- **Client credentials**: machine-to-machine, no user.
- **Device code**: TVs and CLIs ("enter this code on your phone").
- **Implicit** and **resource owner password** grants: deprecated; do not use.

quiz.q: What does OAuth 2.0 mainly provide?
quiz.explain: OAuth grants apps scoped access tokens on the user's behalf.

quiz.q: Which token tells the app who the user is in OpenID Connect?
quiz.explain: The ID token is a JWT describing the authenticated user.

quiz.q: What does PKCE protect against?
options: A stolen authorization code being exchanged by an attacker
quiz.explain: Only the client that holds the code_verifier can exchange the code.

lessons.task: Draw the authorization code + PKCE flow for "Sign in with Google" in a notes app. Show the browser, the notes app backend, Google's authorization server and Google's API as four boxes, and number every arrow (redirect, login, consent, code, token exchange, API call). Mark where `state`, `code_challenge` and `code_verifier` appear.

lessons.title: Multi-factor authentication
lessons.summary: Add a second factor and see exactly how authenticator app codes are generated.

slides.title: Why one factor is not enough
slides.text:
Passwords get **phished**, **reused** and **leaked**.

A second factor means a stolen password alone is **not enough**.

MFA blocks the vast majority of automated account takeovers.
slides.narration: Passwords leak in many ways. Multi factor authentication adds a second, different proof, so a stolen password alone no longer opens the account. Large providers report that MFA blocks the vast majority of automated account takeover attempts.

slides.title: Kinds of second factors
slides.text:
From weaker to stronger:
- **SMS / email codes** (SIM swap, phishing)
- **TOTP apps** (Google/Microsoft Authenticator, password managers)
- **push approval** (watch out for push fatigue)
- **passkeys / security keys** (phishing-resistant)
slides.narration: Not all factors are equal. SMS codes are better than nothing but can be stolen through SIM swapping. Authenticator apps that show six digit codes are stronger. Push notifications are convenient, but attackers spam them hoping you tap approve. The strongest are passkeys and hardware security keys, because they resist phishing.

slides.title: How TOTP works
slides.text:
Phone and server share a **secret** (the QR code).

Every **30 seconds**:
1. `counter = unix_time // 30`
2. `HMAC-SHA1(secret, counter)`
3. pick 4 bytes, take **6 digits**
slides.narration: Authenticator apps use TOTP, the time based one time password standard. When you scan the QR code, your phone and the server store the same secret. Every thirty seconds both sides compute an HMAC of the current time step with that secret and turn it into six digits. If the digits match, the code is accepted.

slides.title: TOTP in Python
slides.text: The whole algorithm (RFC 6238):
slides.code:
def totp(secret_b32, now):
    key = base64.b32decode(secret_b32)
    msg = struct.pack('>Q', now // 30)
    d = hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha1).digest()
    o = d[-1] & 0x0F
    n = int.from_bytes(d[o:o + 4], 'big') & 0x7FFFFFFF
    return str(n % 1_000_000).zfill(6)
slides.narration: Here is the whole algorithm in a few lines of Python. Decode the base32 secret, pack the counter as eight bytes, compute the HMAC, use the last nibble as an offset, and keep six digits.

slides.title: Doing MFA well
slides.text:
- accept ±1 time step for clock drift
- block **code reuse** and rate-limit guesses
- give **recovery codes** at setup
- protect account recovery as strongly as login
- encourage **passkeys**
slides.narration: A few details matter. Accept codes from one step before or after to handle clock drift, but never accept the same code twice, and limit guesses. Give users recovery codes when they enroll. And remember: if the reset password flow skips MFA, attackers will simply use that door.

lessons.notes:
## What MFA is

**Multi-factor authentication** requires proofs from at least two different categories: something you know, have or are.

## Options compared

| Method | Phishing-resistant | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SMS / voice code | no | SIM-swap and interception risk; better than nothing |
| Email code / magic link | no | only as strong as the email account |
| TOTP app | no | offline, standard (RFC 6238), widely supported |
| Push approval | no | use **number matching** to stop push fatigue |
| Passkey / FIDO2 security key | **yes** | bound to the real website |

## TOTP details (RFC 6238)

- Shared secret, usually 160 bits, shown as **base32** in a QR code (`otpauth://totp/...`).
- `T = floor(unix_time / 30)`.
- `HOTP(K, T) = truncate(HMAC-SHA1(K, T))` → 6 digits.
- **Dynamic truncation**: offset = last byte & 0x0F; take 4 bytes there, clear the top bit, `mod 10^6`.

Python library: `pyotp` (`pyotp.TOTP(secret).verify(code)`).

## Server-side rules

- Store the TOTP secret **encrypted**.
- Allow a window of ±1 step; remember the last used step to stop replays.
- Rate-limit attempts (e.g. 5 tries, then delay).
- Provide one-time **recovery codes**, stored hashed.
- Require re-authentication with MFA before changing email, password or MFA settings.
- Make account recovery at least as strong as login.

## Adaptive (risk-based) MFA

Many systems ask for the second factor only when something looks unusual: new device, new country, sensitive action. This balances security and convenience.

quiz.q: Which second factor resists phishing?
quiz.explain: Passkeys are bound to the real website origin, so a fake site cannot use them.

quiz.q: In TOTP, what changes every 30 seconds?
quiz.explain: The counter is unix_time // 30; the secret stays the same.

quiz.q: What is "push fatigue"?
options: Attackers spamming approval prompts until the user taps Approve
quiz.explain: Number matching and rate limits help defend against it.

exercise.title: Generate a TOTP code
exercise.prompt:
Standard input has two lines: a **base32 secret** and a Unix time **now**.

Print the 6-digit TOTP code (RFC 6238): time step 30 seconds, HMAC-SHA1, dynamic truncation, keep leading zeros.

Steps: `counter = now // 30` packed as 8-byte big-endian (`struct.pack('>Q', counter)`), `d = hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha1).digest()`, `offset = d[-1] & 0x0F`, take 4 bytes from `offset` as a big-endian integer, `& 0x7FFFFFFF`, then `% 1000000`.
exercise.starter:
import sys, base64, hmac, hashlib, struct

secret, now = sys.stdin.read().split()
now = int(now)
key = base64.b32decode(secret)

# compute the code
exercise.solution:
import sys, base64, hmac, hashlib, struct

secret, now = sys.stdin.read().split()
key = base64.b32decode(secret)
msg = struct.pack('>Q', int(now) // 30)
d = hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha1).digest()
offset = d[-1] & 0x0F
n = int.from_bytes(d[offset:offset + 4], 'big') & 0x7FFFFFFF
print(str(n % 1000000).zfill(6))

lessons.title: Passkeys and WebAuthn
lessons.summary: Log in without passwords using public-key cryptography that phishing cannot steal.

slides.title: What is a passkey?
slides.text:
A **passkey** is a key pair made for **one website**:
- **private key** stays on your device / password manager
- **public key** is stored by the website

You unlock it with fingerprint, face or PIN.
slides.narration: A passkey replaces the password with a pair of cryptographic keys made for one specific website. The private key never leaves your device or password manager. The website stores only the public key. To use it, you unlock your device with a fingerprint, your face or a PIN.

slides.title: How login works
slides.text:
1. Server sends a random **challenge**
2. Device checks it is the **real origin**
3. You verify (biometric / PIN)
4. Device **signs** the challenge
5. Server verifies with the **public key**
slides.narration: At login, the server sends a fresh random challenge. Your browser confirms that the request really comes from the registered website, you unlock the passkey, and the device signs the challenge with the private key. The server checks the signature with the stored public key. No shared secret ever crosses the network.

slides.title: Why it beats passwords
slides.text:
- **phishing-resistant**: a fake site has a different origin
- nothing reusable to **leak** from the server
- nothing to **guess** or remember
- built-in MFA: device + biometric/PIN
slides.narration: This design fixes the biggest password problems. A fake look alike website has a different origin, so the passkey simply will not work there. A stolen server database contains only public keys, which are useless to attackers. And because you need the device plus your fingerprint or PIN, a passkey is multi factor by itself.

slides.title: Synced vs device-bound
slides.text:
- **Synced**: in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden... survive a lost phone
- **Device-bound**: on a hardware key like a YubiKey; highest assurance
slides.narration: There are two flavors. Synced passkeys live in your platform or password manager and follow you across devices, so losing a phone is not a disaster. Device bound passkeys live on hardware security keys and never leave them, which high security environments prefer.

slides.title: The WebAuthn API
slides.text: Browsers expose it as `navigator.credentials`:
slides.narration: Developers use the WebAuthn browser API. Create registers a new passkey and get signs a login challenge. In Python, the server side is handled by libraries such as py webauthn, which check the origin, challenge and signature for you.

lessons.notes:
## Passkeys in short

A **passkey** is a FIDO2/WebAuthn credential: a public/private key pair created for one **relying party** (website). The private key is protected by the device's secure hardware or a password manager and unlocked with biometrics or a PIN (**user verification**).

## Registration

1. Server creates `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions`: a random **challenge**, the relying party ID (`example.com`), user info.
2. Browser calls `navigator.credentials.create()`.
3. Authenticator makes a key pair, returns the **public key** and a credential ID.
4. Server verifies the response (challenge, origin) and stores the public key with the user.

## Authentication

1. Server sends a new challenge.
2. Browser calls `navigator.credentials.get()`; the authenticator signs data that includes the challenge and the **origin**.
3. Server verifies the signature with the stored public key and checks the challenge, origin, and user-verification flag.

## Why phishing fails

The browser includes the real origin in the signed data, and passkeys are scoped to their relying party ID. A page at `examp1e-login.com` cannot ask for the `example.com` passkey.

## Synced and device-bound

| Type | Where it lives | Pros |
|---|---|---|
| Synced | Apple, Google, Microsoft, password managers | easy recovery, works across devices |
| Device-bound | hardware security keys | strongest, cannot be copied |

## Building it

- Use a well-maintained library: `py_webauthn` (Python), `SimpleWebAuthn` (JavaScript), or your identity provider's built-in support.
- Allow several passkeys per account and a safe recovery path.
- Use **conditional UI** (`autocomplete="username webauthn"`) so passkeys appear in the browser's autofill.
- Keep a fallback during rollout, but make passkeys the easy default.

quiz.q: What does a website store for a passkey?
quiz.explain: Only the public key is stored, so a server breach leaks nothing reusable.

quiz.q: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
options: They are bound to the real website origin
quiz.explain: The browser and authenticator refuse to use a passkey on a different origin.

quiz.q: Which browser API creates a passkey?
quiz.explain: WebAuthn registration uses navigator.credentials.create().

lessons.task: If you have an account at a service that supports passkeys (Google, Microsoft, Apple, GitHub and many others do), add a passkey to it. Then write down: where the passkey is stored, how you unlock it, and what you would do if you lost that device.

lessons.title: Roles and permissions
lessons.summary: Decide who may do what with RBAC, least privilege and per-record checks.

slides.title: Authorization models
slides.text:
- **RBAC**: users get **roles**, roles get **permissions**
- **ABAC**: rules on attributes (department, time, owner)
- **ReBAC**: relationships ("editor of this doc")
slides.narration: After we know who the user is, we must decide what they may do. The most common model is role based access control: users get roles, and roles carry permissions. Attribute based control uses rules about properties, and relationship based control, used by systems like Google Docs, looks at links such as editor of this document.

slides.title: RBAC example
slides.text:
`viewer`: read
`editor`: read, write
`admin`: read, write, delete, manage_users

User `bo` has roles editor + viewer → **read, write**
slides.narration: Here is a small RBAC setup. Viewers can read, editors can read and write, admins can do everything. A user can hold several roles, and their permissions are simply all the permissions of all their roles combined.

slides.title: Principles
slides.text:
- **deny by default**
- **least privilege**: only what is needed
- check on the **server**, every request
- check permissions, not role names, in code
slides.narration: Three principles guide good authorization. Deny by default, so forgetting a rule means no access rather than full access. Give each user only the permissions they need. And check on the server for every request. In code, ask can this user write, rather than is this user an admin, so roles can change without rewriting logic.

slides.title: Check the record too (IDOR)
slides.text:
`GET /invoices/1002`

Role says "can read invoices"...
...but is invoice 1002 **yours**?

Missing this check = **IDOR**, a top cause of breaches.
slides.narration: Roles are not enough. If any customer may read invoices, nothing stops Ana from changing the number in the URL and reading Bo's invoice, unless you also check that the record belongs to her. This bug is called an insecure direct object reference, and it is one of the most common real world vulnerabilities.

slides.title: Growing up
slides.text:
- policy engines: **OPA**, **Cedar**, **OpenFGA**
- audit logs for permission changes
- review access regularly
- separate admin interfaces
slides.narration: As systems grow, teams move rules into dedicated policy engines like Open Policy Agent, Cedar or OpenFGA. They log every permission change, review who has access on a schedule, and keep powerful admin tools separate and extra protected.

lessons.notes:
## RBAC (role-based access control)

```
users ──< user_roles >── roles ──< role_permissions >── permissions
```

- A **permission** is an action: `invoice:read`, `invoice:refund`.
- A **role** bundles permissions: `support_agent`, `accountant`, `admin`.
- A **user** can have several roles; effective permissions are the **union**.

## Other models

- **ABAC**: decisions use attributes. "Doctors may read records of patients in their own ward during their shift."
- **ReBAC**: decisions follow relationships, like Google Zanzibar. "Users who are editors of the folder may edit files inside it." OpenFGA and SpiceDB implement this.

## Principles

1. **Deny by default.**
2. **Least privilege**: give the minimum, remove what is unused.
3. **Enforce on the server**, in one central place (middleware or a policy function).
4. **Check ownership** for every record (`invoice.customer_id == current_user.id`). Missing checks cause IDOR / broken object-level authorization.
5. **Separation of duties**: the person who requests a payment should not approve it.
6. **Log** sensitive actions and permission changes.

## Python sketch

```python
def require(user, perm, record=None):
    if perm not in user.permissions:
        raise Forbidden()
    if record is not None and record.owner_id != user.id and 'admin' not in user.roles:
        raise Forbidden()
```

Return **403** when a logged-in user lacks permission. For records they should not even know exist, many APIs return **404** instead, so attackers cannot discover valid IDs.

quiz.q: In RBAC, permissions are attached to...
quiz.explain: Users receive roles; roles carry permissions.

quiz.q: What does "deny by default" mean?
options: Everyone is an admin until changed
If no rule allows an action, it is refused
quiz.explain: Missing rules should result in no access.

quiz.q: Ana changes /invoices/1001 to /invoices/1002 and sees Bo's invoice. What is this bug?
quiz.explain: The server checked the role but not ownership of the specific record.

lessons.title: Common attacks and defenses
lessons.summary: Recognize brute force, credential stuffing, XSS and CSRF, and stop each one.

slides.title: Guessing attacks
slides.text:
- **Brute force**: try many passwords on one account
- **Password spraying**: one common password on many accounts
- **Credential stuffing**: reuse leaked email+password pairs

Defend: **rate limits**, MFA, breached-password checks, bot detection.
slides.narration: Many attacks are just guessing at scale. Brute force hammers one account. Password spraying tries one common password against many accounts. Credential stuffing replays email and password pairs leaked from other sites. Rate limiting, MFA, breached password checks and bot detection together make these attacks expensive.

slides.title: Do not help attackers
slides.text:
- same message for wrong email **or** password: *"Invalid email or password"*
- slow down after failures instead of a hard permanent lock
- notify users of new-device logins
slides.narration: Do not give attackers hints. Use the same error whether the email or the password was wrong, so they cannot discover which accounts exist. Prefer growing delays over permanent lockouts, which attackers can abuse to lock out real users. And tell users when a new device signs in.

slides.title: XSS: cross-site scripting
slides.text:
Attacker gets **their script** to run on **your page**.

`<script>steal(document.cookie)</script>` saved as a comment...

Defend: **escape output**, use templates that auto-escape, **Content-Security-Policy**, HttpOnly cookies.
slides.narration: Cross site scripting happens when attacker controlled text ends up in your page as code. For example, a comment containing a script tag that runs for every visitor and steals their data. The main defense is escaping output, turning special characters into harmless text. Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add extra layers.

slides.title: Escaping in Python
slides.text: Turn `< > & " '` into HTML entities:
slides.narration: In Python, html dot escape converts the five dangerous characters into safe entities. Modern template engines like Jinja2 and frameworks like React do this automatically, so the danger is mostly in code that bypasses them.

slides.title: CSRF: cross-site request forgery
slides.text:
A malicious site makes **your browser** send a request to a site where you are logged in, **with your cookies**.

Defend: **SameSite** cookies, **CSRF tokens**, check the `Origin` header, never change data with GET.
slides.narration: Cross site request forgery tricks your own browser. While you are logged in to your bank, an evil page submits a hidden form to the bank, and the browser attaches your cookies. Defenses are SameSite cookies, a secret CSRF token in every form, checking the Origin header, and never changing data on a GET request.

slides.title: And more
slides.text:
- **SQL injection** → parameterized queries
- **session hijacking** → HTTPS, HttpOnly, rotation
- **clickjacking** → `frame-ancestors` CSP
- **open redirects** → allow-list redirect URLs
slides.narration: There are many more, but the pattern repeats. SQL injection is stopped by parameterized queries. Session hijacking by HTTPS and secure cookies. Clickjacking by forbidding other sites to frame your pages, and open redirects by only allowing known destinations.

lessons.notes:
## Guessing attacks

| Attack | What it does | Key defenses |
|---|---|---|
| Brute force | many guesses on one account | rate limiting, MFA |
| Password spraying | one weak password on many accounts | block common passwords, detect patterns |
| Credential stuffing | leaked pairs from other sites | breached-password checks, MFA, bot detection |

Use generic error messages, progressive delays, CAPTCHAs or proof-of-work only when suspicious, and alerts on unusual sign-ins.

## XSS (cross-site scripting)

Types: **stored** (saved in the database), **reflected** (from the URL), **DOM-based** (client-side JavaScript).

Defenses:

- **Escape** output for the right context (HTML, attribute, URL, JavaScript).
- Use auto-escaping templates (Jinja2, Django, React); avoid `innerHTML` / `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with user data.
- Sanitize rich HTML with a library such as DOMPurify or nh3.
- **Content-Security-Policy** to block inline scripts.
- **HttpOnly** cookies so scripts cannot read sessions.

```python
import html
safe = html.escape(user_text)   # & < > " ' become entities
```

## CSRF (cross-site request forgery)

The attacker's page causes a state-changing request to your site; the browser adds the user's cookies.

Defenses:

- `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` cookies.
- A random **CSRF token** in forms, checked on the server (frameworks like Django include this).
- Check `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-Site` headers.
- Only change state on POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, never GET.

APIs that use `Authorization: Bearer` headers instead of cookies are not exposed to classic CSRF, because browsers do not add those headers automatically.

## Learn more

The **OWASP Cheat Sheet Series** has short, practical guides for each of these attacks.

quiz.q: An attacker tries "Winter2026!" against 10,000 accounts. This is...
quiz.explain: Spraying uses one common password across many accounts to avoid lockouts.

quiz.q: What is the main defense against XSS?
quiz.explain: Escaping turns attacker text into harmless characters instead of code.

quiz.q: Why does SameSite=Lax help against CSRF?
options: Browsers do not send the cookie on cross-site POST requests
It hides the cookie from JavaScript
quiz.explain: Lax cookies are withheld from cross-site subrequests and form posts.

exercise.title: Escape user comments
exercise.prompt:
You are rendering user comments into an HTML page. For **each line** of standard input, print the escaped line, replacing:

- `&` with `&` (do this first!)
- `<` with `<`
- `>` with `>`
- `"` with `"`
- `'` with `'`

Keep empty lines as empty lines, but do not print anything extra after the last line.
exercise.starter:
import sys

for line in sys.stdin.read().split('\n'):
    # escape and print
    pass
exercise.solution:
import sys

text = sys.stdin.read()
if text.endswith('\n'):
    text = text[:-1]
for line in text.split('\n'):
    line = (line.replace('&', '&').replace('<', '<').replace('>', '>')
                .replace('"', '"').replace("'", '''))
    print(line)

lessons.title: Storing secrets safely
lessons.summary: Keep API keys, passwords and signing keys out of code and under control.

slides.title: What counts as a secret
slides.text:
- database passwords
- API keys (payments, email, AI services)
- JWT signing keys, OAuth client secrets
- encryption keys, private certificates

If it leaks, someone can **act as you**.
slides.narration: A secret is anything that lets someone act as your application: database passwords, API keys, token signing keys, OAuth client secrets and private keys. If one leaks, an attacker can read your data or run up your cloud bill in minutes.

slides.title: Never in Git
slides.text:
Bots scan public repos **within seconds** for keys.

- keep secrets in `.env`, add `.env` to `.gitignore`
- turn on **secret scanning** (GitHub push protection, gitleaks)
- leaked? **revoke and rotate** first, clean history second
slides.narration: Never commit secrets. Bots scan public repositories constantly and find leaked keys within seconds. Keep them in an environment file that Git ignores, and turn on secret scanning so a mistake gets blocked before it is pushed. If a key does leak, revoke and replace it immediately. Deleting the commit is not enough.

slides.title: Reading them in Python
slides.text: Use environment variables:
slides.code:
import os

DB_URL = os.environ['DATABASE_URL']        # crash early if missing
API_KEY = os.environ.get('MAIL_API_KEY')
if not API_KEY:
    raise RuntimeError('MAIL_API_KEY is not set')
slides.narration: In code, read secrets from environment variables. Failing loudly when one is missing is better than running with an empty key. For local development, a dot env file can fill these variables.

slides.title: Secret managers
slides.text:
In production use a **secret manager**:
- AWS Secrets Manager
- Azure Key Vault
- Google Secret Manager
- HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao

Access control, audit logs, **rotation**.
slides.narration: In production, store secrets in a dedicated secret manager. The big clouds each have one, and Vault or its open source fork OpenBao work anywhere. They control who can read each secret, log every access, and can rotate secrets automatically.

slides.title: Even better: no long-lived secrets
slides.text:
- **workload identity**: cloud gives your app short-lived credentials
- **OIDC** from CI (e.g. GitHub Actions) instead of stored cloud keys
- **KMS** to hold encryption keys you never see
slides.narration: The best secret is one you never have to store. Cloud platforms can give your running app short lived credentials automatically, and CI systems like GitHub Actions can log in to clouds with OIDC instead of stored keys. For encryption, a key management service keeps the master keys inside protected hardware.

slides.title: Generating secrets
slides.text: Use the `secrets` module, **not** `random`:
slides.code:
import secrets
print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))   # API key / reset token
print(secrets.token_hex(32))       # 256-bit key as hex
slides.narration: When you need a new random secret, such as a token or an API key, use Python's secrets module. The random module is predictable and must never be used for security.

lessons.notes:
## Where secrets should (not) live

| Place | OK? |
|---|---|
| Source code / Git history | **never** |
| Frontend JavaScript or mobile app bundle | **never** (anyone can extract them) |
| Logs, error messages, screenshots, chat | **never** |
| `.env` file on a dev machine (git-ignored) | fine for development |
| Environment variables injected by the platform | good |
| Secret manager (AWS, Azure, Google, Vault/OpenBao) | best for production |
| Short-lived credentials via workload identity / OIDC | even better |

## Practical rules

1. **Add `.env` to `.gitignore`** before your first commit. Commit a `.env.example` with fake values.
2. **Enable secret scanning** and push protection on your repositories.
3. **Least privilege**: each key gets only the scopes it needs (read-only where possible).
4. **Rotate** regularly and immediately after any suspected leak.
5. **Separate** secrets per environment (dev, staging, production).
6. **Audit** who accessed what.

## Encryption at rest

- Encrypt sensitive data (e.g. TOTP secrets, tokens) in the database with a key from a **KMS** (envelope encryption).
- Use well-known libraries such as `cryptography` (Fernet or AES-GCM). Never invent your own cipher.

## Random values in Python

```python
import secrets
reset_token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
```

Store only a **hash** of reset tokens and API keys you issue, just like passwords, so a database leak does not expose them.

## If a secret leaks

1. Revoke / rotate it **now**.
2. Check logs for misuse.
3. Remove it from history (`git filter-repo`) and fix the process that leaked it.

quiz.q: A secret key was pushed to a public repo. What do you do first?
options: Make the repo private and forget it
quiz.explain: Bots may already have copied it; only revoking makes it useless.

quiz.q: Which Python module should generate tokens?
quiz.explain: secrets uses a cryptographically secure random generator.

quiz.q: Why not put an API key in frontend JavaScript?
options: Anyone can read the code and extract the key
quiz.explain: Everything sent to the browser is visible to users.

lessons.task: Audit a project of yours (or an imaginary one): search for strings like `password=`, `api_key`, `secret`, `token` in the code. Write a plan that moves every secret into environment variables, adds a `.env.example`, and lists which secret manager you would use in production and how often you would rotate each secret.

lessons.title: Authentication in professional practice
lessons.summary: Put it all together: build vs buy, account recovery, monitoring and security standards.

slides.title: Build or buy?
slides.text:
**Identity providers**: Auth0 / Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, AWS Cognito, Google Identity Platform, Clerk, **Keycloak** (self-hosted)

They bring MFA, passkeys, OAuth/OIDC, SSO, audits.
slides.narration: Authentication is hard to get right, so many teams use an identity provider. Hosted services like Auth0, Entra ID, Cognito or Clerk, or self hosted Keycloak, give you MFA, passkeys, social login and single sign on out of the box. Even then, authorization inside your app is still your job.

slides.title: Account recovery is a login
slides.text:
- reset links: random, **single-use**, short expiry, stored **hashed**
- same response whether the email exists or not
- notify the user after changes
- recovery codes for MFA users
slides.narration: Attackers love password reset flows, because they are often weaker than login. Reset tokens must be random, single use, short lived and stored hashed. Respond the same way whether or not the email exists, and notify users when their password or MFA settings change.

slides.title: Log and watch
slides.text:
Log security events:
- logins, failures, MFA changes
- password resets, role changes

Alert on spikes and impossible travel.
**Never** log passwords or tokens.
slides.narration: You cannot defend what you cannot see. Log security events such as logins, failures, password resets and role changes, and alert on spikes or suspicious patterns. Just never put passwords, tokens or full secrets in those logs.

slides.title: Standards and checklists
slides.text:
- **OWASP ASVS** (v5): what to verify
- **OWASP Cheat Sheets**: how to build it
- **NIST SP 800-63**: identity guidelines
- threat modeling: *what can go wrong?*
slides.narration: Professionals do not rely on memory. The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard lists what a secure app must do, the OWASP cheat sheets show how, and NIST special publication eight hundred sixty three covers digital identity. Before building a feature, run a quick threat model: what are we building, what can go wrong, and what will we do about it.

slides.title: Your security habit list
slides.text:
1. use proven libraries
2. HTTPS + secure cookies
3. strong hashing (Argon2id)
4. MFA, ideally passkeys
5. authorize every request
6. secrets out of code
7. keep dependencies updated
8. test: scanners, reviews, pen tests
slides.narration: Let us finish with a habit list. Use proven libraries, serve everything over HTTPS with secure cookies, hash passwords with Argon2id, offer MFA and passkeys, authorize every request on the server, keep secrets out of code, update dependencies, and test your security with scanners, code reviews and penetration tests.

lessons.notes:
## Build vs buy

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| Framework built-in (Django auth, Laravel, ASP.NET Identity) | simple, in your code | you maintain MFA, passkeys, SSO |
| Self-hosted IdP (Keycloak, Authentik, Zitadel) | full control, standards-based | you operate and patch it |
| Hosted IdP (Auth0/Okta, Entra ID, Cognito, Clerk, Firebase Auth) | fast, many features | cost, vendor lock-in |

Whatever you choose, your app still does **authorization** and must validate tokens correctly.

## Account lifecycle

- **Sign-up**: verify email, check breached passwords, offer passkeys.
- **Login**: rate-limit, MFA, notify new devices.
- **Recovery**: single-use, hashed, short-lived tokens; re-check MFA; notify after changes.
- **Session management**: list active sessions, "log out everywhere".
- **Deletion**: remove data and revoke tokens.

## Single sign-on (SSO)

Companies want employees to log in once with their corporate identity. Support **OIDC** and often **SAML 2.0**, and **SCIM** to sync user accounts automatically.

## Security monitoring

Log: successful and failed logins, MFA enrollments, password and email changes, role changes, token revocations. Send them to a central system and alert on anomalies.

## Testing

- Automated scanners (SAST, dependency scanning, DAST such as OWASP ZAP).
- Code review with a security checklist (OWASP ASVS).
- Periodic penetration tests and, for larger products, a bug bounty program.

## Threat modeling in four questions

1. What are we working on?
2. What can go wrong?
3. What are we going to do about it?
4. Did we do a good job?

Ask them for every new feature that touches login, permissions or secrets.

quiz.q: Even with a hosted identity provider, what remains your app's job?
quiz.explain: The IdP authenticates; deciding what each user may do in your app is still yours.

quiz.q: How should password reset tokens be stored?
quiz.explain: Treat them like passwords: hash them and limit their lifetime and use.

quiz.q: What is OWASP ASVS?
options: A standard listing security requirements to verify
quiz.explain: The Application Security Verification Standard lists what a secure application should do.
